results.title: The GPU you can rent today costs a third of the hyperscaler's. The one you have to reserve for three years is the actual decision. | Aaron Jones
highlights:
The GPU you can rent today costs a third of the hyperscaler's. The one you have to reserve for three years is the actual decision.

AWS just raised its GPU Capacity Block prices again on July 1, its second hike in six months, roughly 20% (SDxCentral, 2026). H200 blocks now run near $39/hr and Blackwell reaches about $14 per GPU-hour. AWS's own CEO admits they are "still running six-year-old A100 servers" because demand outruns supply. Microsoft has acknowledged mid-size enterprises hitting Azure GPU quota limits and multi-month waits, and volume B200 orders carry 12 to 18 month backlogs (Spheron, 2026). Meanwhile neoclouds list B200 on-demand around $5/hr (Lambda $4.99, Nebius $5.50) against up to $14/hr on hyperscaler blocks, with capacity you can light up this week.

The case for renting neocloud now: price and availability today beat the queue. If your model is ready and your competitor is on a waitlist, the provider that hands you B200s this week is not a shortcut, it is the whole race. Growth compounds from shipping, not from waiting for a reservation window.

The case against, the trap: the $5 on-demand rate is bait. Real reserved capacity comes with multi-year lock-in. CoreWeave's up-to-60% discounts and $66B backlog are years of committed spend, and a five-year contract to a young provider is counterparty and durability risk, not flexibility. You can trade a hyperscaler queue for a lock-in you cannot unwind.

results.title: Blackwell Normalizes — and the H200 Joins the Repricing Conversation - GPU Resource
highlights:
For most of 2025, Blackwell allocations moved through a familiar gating mechanism: constrained NVLink fabric supply, HBM3e binning, and tight CoWoS packaging capacity kept lead times elevated and spot premiums intact. That equilibrium has shifted. By mid-2026, TSMC CoWoS-L throughput has scaled to a point where GB200 and B200 availability is no longer the exception for hyperscale and Tier-2 cloud buyers. Lead times on B200 SXM configurations have compressed from 26+ weeks to the 8–12 week window that, historically, signals the transition from allocation scarcity to commodity-adjacent inventory management.

This is what normalization looks like in the GPU market — not a collapse in demand, but a structural shift in who holds pricing power. The GPU Pulse Report has been tracking B200 spot price erosion quarter-over-quarter; the trajectory is consistent with the H100 normalization curve that played out across Q3–Q4 2023, roughly 18 months after that architecture’s initial ramp.

## The H200: Secondary Repricing Begins

What the H100/A100 repricing story established is a reliable cascade: once a successor architecture normalizes, the prior-generation flagship undergoes a re-rating — not to scrap value, but to a new equilibrium that reflects its workload fit rather than its scarcity premium.

The H200 is entering that phase now. Introduced as a bridging upgrade over the H100 (principally the HBM3e memory upgrade delivering roughly 2× memory bandwidth), the H200 carried a significant premium through its ramp cycle. With Blackwell readily available and B200 per-FLOP economics increasingly competitive, the H200’s addressable use cases are narrowing to a specific stratum: inference-heavy deployments where memory bandwidth is the binding constraint, racks already configured for SXM5 that lack the power and cooling headroom for a full Blackwell upgrade, and cost-sensitive buyers who don’t require NVLink Switch interconnect at scale.

Outside those niches, the incentive to specify H200 over B200 is weakening. Spot pricing data — covered in depth in our Industry Analysis section — shows H200 on-demand rates beginning to track below the premium floor established in 2025.

...

The H100/A100 repricing arc is the clearest precedent. When H100 normalized in late 2023, A100 spot rates fell sharply within two quarters — but stabilized above zero, anchored by PyTorch ecosystem compatibility, existing CUDA workloads, and data-center operators unwilling to absorb the capex of a full fleet refresh. A100 settled into a durable secondary market, heavily weighted toward fine-tuning workloads, academic compute, and cost-optimized inference at modest context lengths.

The H200 will follow a structurally similar path, but with one difference: its workload window is narrower than the A100’s was. The A100 had a multi-year installed base and broad framework support by the time H100 displaced it. The H200’s installed base is shallower. Secondary market absorption will be faster, and the price floor may settle lower relative to its original MSRP than the A100’s did.

For procurement teams, this has a direct implication: H200 secondary-market assets acquired at post-normalization pricing can be highly cost-effective for memory-bandwidth-bound inference pipelines. The GPU Industry News feed is tracking active fleet disposition announcements as hyperscalers begin rotating H200 capacity.

...

The key leading indicators for the next repricing move — whether the H200 floor drops further or stabilizes — are HBM3e spot pricing (shared with B200 supply), hyperscaler Q3 capex guidance, and CoWoS allocation signals from TSMC. If CoWoS-L output continues to outpace Blackwell demand, downward pressure on both B200 and H200 pricing will persist. If demand-side acceleration (driven by inference scaling, agent infrastructure, and multimodal workloads) absorbs the added supply, a new equilibrium forms earlier than the H100 precedent would suggest.

results.title: Neocloud | AI Wiki
highlights:
A neocloud is a cloud computing company whose business is renting out GPU capacity for artificial intelligence workloads, rather than selling the broad catalogue of storage, database, networking and application services that defines a general purpose cloud. The research firm SemiAnalysis set out the widely cited definition in an October 2024 report, describing an AI Neocloud as "a new breed of cloud compute provider focused on offering GPU compute rental" [1].

Reference rental price per chip

| Chip | Reference price | Cheapest on demand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B300 | $9.50/GPU·hr Typical, median of 3 specialist clouds | $7.40 |
| B200 | $7.44/GPU·hr Typical, median of 4 specialist clouds | $6.00 |
| H200 | $5.40/GPU·hr Typical, median of 3 specialist clouds | $3.99 |
| H100 | $3.99/GPU·hr Typical, median of 4 specialist clouds | $3.20 |
| A100 80GB | $1.35-$2.79/GPU·hr Typical, range of 2 specialist clouds | $1.35 |
| MI300X | $6.00/GPU·hr Big-cloud list price | $2.99 |

AI Compute Tracker is a companion site owned and operated by the same team as AI Wiki. Posted list prices, not transactions. Data: AI Compute Tracker (aicomputetracker.com), CC BY 4.0; third-party terms apply to data from Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, GPU cloud pricing pages, Beam, Chip vendor documentation.

...

Two supply constraints created the opening. The first was the scarcity of high-end accelerators relative to demand, the condition SemiAnalysis was already mapping when it described the neocloud build-out in 2024 [1] and which returned as an acute shortage in 2026, when on-demand rental capacity sold out across GPU types [22].

...

Smaller operators including Voltage Park, RunPod and Vast.ai occupy the on-demand end of the market, selling capacity without a long-term commitment rather than by the year. Voltage Park advertises a single H100 for one hour with no contract [32], RunPod prices dedicated GPU pods by the hour [33], and Vast.ai runs a marketplace whose prices are set by supply and demand across more than 40 data centers and billed by the second [34].

...

### Price and refinancing risk

Rental prices have moved sharply in both directions. SemiAnalysis observed meaningful declines in on-demand GPU pricing as early as its October 2024 report [1], and rates for H100 capacity kept falling into 2025 before reversing: SemiAnalysis reported that one-year H100 rental contract pricing rose almost 40% from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, with on-demand capacity sold out across GPU types and all capacity coming online until August to September 2026 already booked [22]. For an operator whose debt is fixed and whose contracts are signed years ahead, that volatility cuts both ways.

results.title: NVIDIA B200 Cloud Pricing and Availability Guide
highlights:
## Cloud B200 pricing is a band, not a single sticker

NVIDIA B200 cloud rental is commonly sold as a per-GPU-hour charge for dedicated Blackwell capacity, with public on-demand list levels often landing in the mid-single-digit dollars per GPU-hour depending on provider, region, and commit. That is the practical answer to "how much per hour," but it is incomplete until you pin the commercial container around the number. Four variables move the rate before a contract is even signed:

- Billing model: On-demand, reserved or committed capacity, spot or interruptible inventory, and custom enterprise commits produce different unit rates for the same chip.
- SKU shape: Single-GPU listings, 2/4-GPU nodes, and 8-GPU SXM systems rarely invoice like a one-line "B200" tile. Per-GPU math looks attractive until you must take a full HGX-style node.
- What the hour includes: Some rate cards are GPU-only; others bundle host CPU/RAM, disk, or fabric differently. Egress, shared filesystems, and managed Kubernetes add lines that never appear in the headline figure.
- Stock class: Limited, waitlist, and region-locked inventory is often priced as if it were elastic. A low number on a sold-out SKU is not a sourcing plan.

Cross-provider indexes that scrape public listings currently show B200 quotes spanning from the low-$3 per GPU-hour range on aggressive reserved inventory up through mid-single digits on typical on-demand rows, with scarce bundles climbing higher. Treat those indexes as a market envelope, not an SLA. The real decision is which point on that envelope is buyable for your region, isolation level, and run length.

We publish dedicated NVIDIA GPU list pricing for production AI, including B200 at from $4.00 per GPU-hour under Limited Availability, alongside H100 at from $2.00 and H200 at from $2.60 per GPU-hour. That row is useful because it is checkable on our pricing page rather than implied by a private quote.

One boundary to keep clear: renting B200 GPUs by the hour is not the same commercial object as renting a GB200 NVL72 rack. B200 answers "per-GPU Blackwell capacity for training and inference nodes." NVL72 answers "liquid-cooled, rack-scale system with a different interconnect and power envelope." Collapse those into one spreadsheet cell and your per-hour and lead-time comparisons will be wrong.

...

## Where B200 rental fits next to H100 and H200

A B200 shortlist should always be scored against the generation you can already buy in volume. In our current published listings the dedicated starting ladder is deliberately simple:

| NVIDIA GPU | GMI Cloud list rate | Availability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | from $2.00 / GPU-hour | Available now |
| H200 | from $2.60 / GPU-hour | Available now |
| B200 | from $4.00 / GPU-hour | Limited Availability |
| GB200 NVL72 | from $8.00 / GPU-hour | Available now (rack-scale) |

That ladder does not by itself prove B200 is worth it; it frames the premium you pay for Blackwell memory and bandwidth versus staying on Hopper. Stay on H100 or H200 when the model and batch plan already clear your latency and throughput targets, when depth of stock this week matters more than peak chip performance, or when your stack is tuned on Hopper and migration cost dominates chip savings. Move toward B200 when you are memory- or bandwidth-bound on H200 for the target model size, when utilization will be high enough that throughput-per-dollar absorbs the higher sticker rate, or when you need a vendor that will discuss limited B200 allocation honestly instead of advertising infinite supply.

...

If you only bookmark the lowest B200 hourly screenshot, you still do not know whether you can ship; if you only ask "do you have Blackwell," you still do not know the burn rate. Close the loop in one pass: ask for a unit rate, a stock status, a region, and an isolation mode together. In our current published materials, B200 begins at $4.00 per GPU-hour with Limited Availability, while H100 and H200 remain the deeper stock rungs for workloads that do not yet pay for Blackwell. Re-check the live pricing page at order time, convert hours into monthly burn at your utilization, and escalate to reserved Prime Inference capacity when production latency cannot tolerate cold starts.

H100 one-year contracts are up about 40% from their October low, from roughly $1.70 an hour to $2.35. The same card on the spot market still trades close to two-thirds below its 2023 peak.

Those two numbers are supposed to disagree, but they do not.

The debate everyone is having about AI compute is collapse-or-boom: either the buildout is a bubble that pops, or demand is infinite and the capex is justified. The contract-versus-spot split says both sides are watching the wrong number. What is scarce is not chips. It is committed, reliable capacity, and it is getting more expensive precisely while uncommitted spot gets cheaper. The shortage moved from the silicon to the guarantee.

The fair counter is real, so here it is: Spot really is soft, and the melting-asset story has a point. CoreWeave's own 2020-era A100s are re-contracting at around 95% of their original rates as they cascade down into inference work, which is not what a melting ice cube does. An H100 bought today will earn for years.

highlights:
RunPod pricing depends first on what stays allocated: a Pod charges while its infrastructure is allocated; Serverless Flex charges while workers run; retained storage can bill after compute stops. A successful request is not the end of the worker’s billable lifetime.

The November 2 check changes the buying math:

- Seven of 13 Flex rates are higher than our October 17 observation. The 24 GB pooled L4-class tier is $0.75/hour, RTX 4090 Pro $1.34/hour, H100 Pro $5.39/hour and B200 $10.79/hour. The largest observed increase is B200 at 24.88%. These are observation-to-observation differences, not a claim that prices changed today.
- All 42 Pod list prices are unchanged from October 17. L4 Secure remains $0.59/hour; A100 PCIe $1.79/hour; H100 PCIe $2.89/hour. More expensive Flex lowers the worker-hours at which an always-on Pod becomes cheaper on compute alone.
- Configuration defaults depend on how you deploy. Current endpoint docs say the console uses a five-second idle timeout while REST v2 uses ten seconds. The same five-second example cannot stand in for both.
- The B300 Flex memory label is now 288 GB, matching the Pod page’s label; the October 17 capture showed 280 GB for Flex. Matching labels still do not prove matching host resources or throughput.
